item.research_question: Do high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit the theoretically predicted sluggish diffusion and enhanced thermal stability, or do they undergo phase separation and structural evolution at high temperatures?
item.material_system: AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy nanoalloys (HENA), specifically near-equimolar compositions (≈Au20Co28Cu11Ni20Pt21) with diameters of 3–6.5 nm.
item.processing_route: Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) on amorphous 50 nm SiN membranes or 5 nm carbon films; substrate temperature 873 K, laser frequency 5 Hz, total nominal thickness 4 nm.
item.test_conditions: In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating from 298 to 973 K (steps at 473, 673, 773, 873, 973 K) with a heating rate of 1 K s⁻¹; MD simulations from 400 to 1500 K using EAM potentials.
key_findings: Particle size distribution remains unchanged at 473 K but widens up to 13 nm at 973 K due to coalescence of smallest NPs (2–4 nm).
NPs reshape from elliptical to spherical shapes as the in-plane shape ratio increases with temperature.
Phase separation occurs progressively with temperature, driven by the segregation of Au and Cu to the NP surface.
At 973 K, a complete loss of gold and copper is observed due to the melting and evaporation of the Au-Cu surface shell.
Coalescence events at 773–873 K enhance atomic diffusion, leading to more pronounced Au-Cu segregation compared to non-coalesced NPs.
Atomic diffusion in AuCoCuNiPt is surprisingly more active than in monometallic (Au, CoPt) and bimetallic (AuCu) subsystems, with coalescence observed at 673 K versus >873 K in subsystems.
MD simulations show surface concentration of Au and Cu becomes predominant above 1000 K, while Ni and Co drop below 0.1% at the surface.
item.mechanism: The segregation is driven by surface energy minimization (cohesion effect) where Au and Cu, having the lowest surface energies, migrate to the surface. This process is kinetically controlled by atomic diffusion, which is accelerated by temperature and significantly boosted by the reshaping and neck formation during coalescence events, rather than being hindered by sluggish diffusion or entropy stabilization.
item.limitations: The study notes that the fabrication time (≈12 min) is shorter than the time required to reach thermodynamic equilibrium at 873 K, meaning the initial FCC structure is kinetically trapped. Additionally, the MD simulations considered only individual atom diffusion and not collective motions during coalescence.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that a surface energy term must be included in the Gibbs free energy formula to explain the atomic structure of small HENA and call for further investigation into how surface effects govern the structural properties and stability of HENA for different applications.
quotes: Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature.

Surprisingly, our in situ TEM observations show that reshaping and coalescence processes are observed at only 673 K in the present HENA, whereas they are observed above 873 K in CoPt, AuCu, and Au NPs.

This result also explains previous reports that revealed the presence of sup‐10 nm core‐shell nanostructures in the FCC AuCoCuNiPt NP assembly with a mean size below 5 nm fabricated by PLD at 873 K, since coalescence is necessary to reach NP size above 10 nm.
